meta.title: The Backrooms: Exit Protocol
meta.notes: 30-section sample with good/bad/special endings that loop back to start.
meta.blurb: You slipped into the Backrooms. Map fragments point to a powered storage facility and a working terminal—if you can rewrite the rules, you can leave.

S01.text:
You were walking down a hallway you’ve walked a thousand times.

Then your foot found nothing—no step, no floor—just a soft give, like reality shrugged.

You dropped through a bad frame of the world and landed on damp carpet under buzzing fluorescent lights.

Yellow walls. Low ceiling. Endless right angles that feel like they were measured by someone who hates you.

You don’t need to say the name out loud to know it.

The Backrooms.

S02.text:
You stand. Your knees complain. The carpet squishes like it’s been wet for years.

You pick a direction and walk. The hum follows you like a thought you can’t shake.

After a few turns, you notice the worst part:

Nothing here feels random. It feels permitted.

S03.text:
You sit and listen. The hum isn’t steady. It rises and falls like breathing.

Far away—too far for this to make sense—footsteps echo once, then stop.

Stillness doesn’t hide you. It announces you.

You taste panic and swallow it.

S04.text:
You walk long enough for time to lose meaning.

Then you find something that doesn’t belong: torn paper taped to a wall at eye level.

A map fragment. Smudged ink. A crude box labeled STORAGE and a line labeled POWER NODE.

Someone else tried to solve this place with planning instead of screaming.

S05.text:
You scrape a line into the wall with a loose screw you found in the carpet.

It’s ugly, but it’s yours.

Ten minutes later, you see the same mark again—same scratch, same height—around a corner that should have been new.

You’re not navigating space.

You're navigating a loop.

S07.text:
You push faster. Faster feels like control.

The lights flicker once, and the hum drops lower, like the building disapproves.

A soft scrape follows behind you—something adjusting its pace to match yours.

You force yourself to breathe through your nose. Slow. Quiet. Human.

S06.text:
The fragment shows a route: three turns, a long corridor, a dead end that isn’t a dead end.

In the margin, someone wrote a note so faint you can barely read it:

“POWER FIRST. EXIT SECOND.”

You don’t know who wrote it, but it reads like a warning from someone who learned the hard way.

S08.text:
You run.

Your footfalls slap wet carpet. Your breath gets loud.

The hum spikes until it feels like it’s inside your teeth.

Something down the hall moves when you move—fast enough to stay out of sight, close enough to be real.

You don’t see it.

You don’t need to.

S09.text:
You follow the fragment’s turns exactly. Left. Right. Right. Straight.

The world resists you in small ways: corners that feel longer than they should, doors that appear where you don’t remember them.

At the end of the corridor you find a metal service door set into concrete walls.

It’s too industrial for this place.

Which makes it feel like truth.

choices.label: LOOK FOR A KEYPAD OR PANEL

S10.text:
You drift off-route and hunt for more paper. You find two more fragments under a loose baseboard.

They don’t make a map so much as a system diagram: corridors grouped into zones, and a note: “STORAGE FEEDS TERMINAL.”

Someone wasn’t just lost here. Someone was mapping infrastructure.

That means there is infrastructure to map.

S11.text:
You duck into a side hall and press your back to the wall.

The hum softens, like the building is listening.

Something passes the end of the hallway. You see only a shadow smear across yellow paint, too tall and too thin.

It pauses. You hold your breath.

Then it moves on.

You don’t move for a full minute after it’s gone.

S12.text:
The handle turns—barely—and then stops like it hit a lock that doesn’t exist.

The door is real metal. Cold. Heavy. Honest.

But it won’t open.

You feel a childish urge to kick it, and you hate yourself for it.

Then you see it: a tiny green LED in the corner of a panel.

Power is near. Not here.

S13.text:
You find a breaker box recessed into the wall a few feet away.

Most switches are down. Some are missing entirely.

One is labeled in faded marker: ZONE C / STORAGE.

It’s the first label you’ve seen that feels like it came from a world with rules.

S14.text:
You spread the fragments on the carpet and press them together like a puzzle.

A path forms—messy but readable—leading from ENTRY LOOP to STORAGE to TERMINAL ROOM.

In the corner, a warning is underlined three times:

“DO NOT EXECUTE EXIT WITHOUT BACKUP.”

You laugh once, sharp and tired.

Backup is a fantasy in a place that doesn’t exist.

S15.text:
The hallway changes. The carpet becomes less wet. The walls look freshly painted, as if the Backrooms is trying to convince you it’s normal.

Then you find a sign bolted to the ceiling: TERMINAL ACCESS — AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL.

A joke. Or a clue.

Below it, a locked door and a dead keypad.

S16.text:
You flip the switch.

The lights stutter like they’re waking up from a long sleep.

A low mechanical whir starts behind the service door.

The green LED brightens. The keypad beside the door comes to life with a faint beep.

For the first time since you fell in, something responds to you like a machine instead of a nightmare.

choices.label: ENTER THE CODE FROM THE FRAGMENT

S17.text:
The fragment had a sequence scribbled in the margin. You type it in slowly, hands steady.

The keypad chirps.

The lock clicks.

The heavy door swings inward on oiled hinges that should not be this well maintained.

Beyond it: shelving, crates, and a smell like cardboard and old plastic.

A storage facility inside a place that shouldn’t have supplies.

S19.text:
You wait in the doorway, listening.

At first: only the hum and your heartbeat.

Then: a distant tapping, like fingers on a plastic table.

It stops when you breathe too loudly.

You step inside anyway, because the alternative is staying in the corridor where you already know you’re being watched.

S18.text:
The shelves are stacked with things that look like they were pulled from offices: keyboards, cables, binders, fluorescent tubes.

Map fragments, too—taped to crate lids, stuck under clipboards, folded into drawers like breadcrumbs.

Someone built a trail.

You find a rolling cart with a clipboard attached.

On the top page: “POWER ROUTE CONFIRMED. TERMINAL IN ZONE D.”

S20.text:
You pocket two more fragments. Your hands shake from adrenaline and relief.

The new pieces show a maintenance corridor labeled ZONE D and a small room icon labeled WORKSTATION.

In the corner: “If the workstation boots, do not panic. It will try to talk to you.”

You stare at that line for a long second.

Then you fold the paper carefully and keep moving.

S21.text:
You follow a thick cable run along the base of the wall, like following a vein.

It snakes through a narrow service corridor where the walls are gray instead of yellow.

The hum changes here—cleaner, more electrical.

You pass a label printed on plastic: “NODE D — LIVE.”

Live means power. Power means systems. Systems mean exits can exist.

choices.label: TURN BACK BEFORE IT CHANGES MORE

S23.text:
You search crates until you find a basic tool kit: a screwdriver set, a headlamp, electrical tape.

No weapons. No comfort. Just maintenance tools, like the Backrooms expects repairs.

In the bottom of the kit is a sticky note:

“THE DOOR ISN’T THE EXIT. THE CODE IS.”

You swallow hard. Your throat feels tight.

You take the tools.

choices.label: TRY TO MAKE A SIGNAL DEVICE

S24.text:
You try to build a signal device from spare parts—something that could ping, something that could call.

The moment you connect the battery, the lights blink twice.

The hum drops.

A new sound enters the air: a soft modem-like chirp, like laughter made of static.

The Backrooms doesn’t like you inventing new behavior inside it.

S22.text:
Zone D begins with a door that’s already ajar, as if someone expected you.

Beyond it: a short hallway and a small operations room with a desk, a chair, and a computer that looks too clean to be real.

The monitor is dark.

The tower of the machine is humming quietly.

It has power.

It has patience.

S26.text:
You search the desk.

A drawer holds a notebook filled with cramped handwriting: attempts, dates, and one repeated phrase: “EXIT DENIED.”

A page is torn out. Another is stained with something brown you don’t want to identify.

In the back, you find a laminated card:

ADMIN LOGIN: GUEST

PASSWORD: (blank)

Under it, someone wrote: “It lies. It always asks twice.”

S25.text:
The monitor flickers on.

A cursor blinks on a black screen.

No welcome message. No icons. Just a command line like an open mouth waiting to be fed.

Text appears on its own, letter by letter:

> IDENTIFY.

You don’t type. The cursor blinks anyway.

> IDENTIFY.

The notebook said it would ask twice.

Now you believe it.

S27.text:
You type your name.

The machine pauses, like it’s tasting it.

New text appears:

> NAME NOT FOUND.

> ASSIGNING TEMPORARY ID.

A new prompt:

> PURPOSE?

The cursor blinks, patient and cruel.

S28.text:
You type: GUEST.

The machine replies:

> GUEST ACCEPTED.

Then, like a trap closing:

> EXIT FUNCTIONS RESTRICTED.

A directory list appears—files and folders named like infrastructure: ZONES, NODES, BOUNDARY, PERMISSIONS.

This is not a haunted computer.

This is a control panel.

And you are in the wrong account.

S29.text:
You open PERMISSIONS.

Lines of code scroll—clean, readable, terrifying.

Rules. Flags. Conditions like a checklist for reality.

One line stands out:

EXIT_ALLOWED = FALSE

Another line references a key file:

BOUNDARY.KEY

You don’t know where that key is.

But you know what you can change.

S30.text:
You attempt to elevate access.

The machine pauses.

> AUTH REQUIRED.

It asks again.

> AUTH REQUIRED.

Your skin prickles. The hum shifts as if the walls are leaning in.

You search directories quickly. In NODES, you find a reference:

BOUNDARY.KEY stored in STORAGE / CRATE 14.

Back where you started.

The Backrooms loves circular jokes.

choices.label: RETURN TO STORAGE FOR THE KEY
FORCE THE EXIT WITHOUT THE KEY

S31.text:
You toggle EXIT_ALLOWED from FALSE to TRUE.

The moment you save the file, the lights in the room dim—not off, just lower, like the building is narrowing its eyes.

The computer prints a single line:

> WARNING: BOUNDARY INTEGRITY UNVERIFIED.

A new command appears:

> EXECUTE EXIT? (Y/N)

Your mouth goes dry.

This is it. Or it’s a trap.

S32.text:
You type: Y.

The hum drops into silence so complete it hurts.

A door appears in the far wall of the operations room, where there has never been a door.

It is plain. Unmarked. The kind of door you would ignore in an office building.

The computer prints one more line:

> STEP THROUGH. DO NOT LOOK BACK.

Your throat tightens.

The simplest instruction is always the hardest.

END_GOOD.text:
GOOD ENDING — EXIT PROTOCOL COMPLETE

You step through.

For one breath, everything is white.

Then you’re on cold concrete in a familiar hallway, your own world’s fluorescent lights buzzing overhead.

People walk past you without noticing. No one screams. No one points.

You stand up slowly, expecting the carpet squish. It isn’t there.

But later—days later—when you stare at a blank terminal, you swear the cursor blinks a little too patiently.

END_BAD.text:
BAD ENDING — PERMISSION DENIED

You push the system too hard. Or you get too loud. Or you trust the wrong door.

The lights flicker, and the corridors rearrange.

The map fragments in your pocket turn to wet pulp.

The hum rises until it fills your skull.

You walk for a long time. Maybe hours. Maybe years.

Eventually you realize the worst part:

The Backrooms didn’t kill you.

It filed you away.

END_SPECIAL.text:
SPECIAL ENDING — THE BACKROOMS LET YOU GO

You wait.

You watch the door breathe—yes, breathe—like it’s deciding what you are.

The computer prints a final line on its own:

> ACCEPTED.

The door opens without a sound.

You wake up in your bed at home, heart racing, sure it was a nightmare—until you check your laptop.

A new folder sits on the desktop: BOUNDARY.

Inside it, a single text file contains one line:

> IDENTIFY.

You don’t remember typing it.

But the cursor is blinking, waiting for you to answer.
